page.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
page.description: A 360M model that pretends to be a terminal, and remembers what you did
page.text_excerpt: simedw@blog $ cat ~/writing/world-model-terminal.md ~/writing ~/projects WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal 2026-10-21 / Simon Edwardsson / Follow @SimEdw / Discuss on HN ↗ TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell. The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly. When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs. Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal. A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print. What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output. The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. AI agents Software careers Future of work In this article Programming has been ending since 1954 What 2026 actually looks like The line that keeps going up When code gets cheap, the queue moves The rung we might be sawing off Five guesses for 2031 Back to Tuesday It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine. While you slept, four agents worked through the backlog you sorted yesterday afternoon. Three of them finished. Their pull requests are waiting for you, each with the tests it added, a short recording of the feature working, and a note about the parts it wasn’t sure of. The fourth agent stopped at 2:13 a.m. and left you a question instead: The spec says refunds go back to the original card. This customer’s card expired in March. What should happen? The agent could write refund code all day long. What it can’t do is decide what your company owes a customer whose card has expired, so it stopped and asked, which is exactly what you’d want from a new hire too. Your morning goes like this: you read three pull requests, you go and talk to someone in support, and you write the rule down so clearly that nobody (human or otherwise) has to guess again. OCTOBER 20, 2026 [Note that this article is a transcript of the video embedded above.] The idea is simple: If there’s a fire in a tall building that blocks the main stairwell, people need an alternative way to evacuate, preferably one that is somewhat protected or at least far away from where the fire is happening. If you’re in a one or two story building, it’s pretty simple: just get out of any window or door. You may get hurt a little, but you’ll still be away from the fire. In the denser cities of the early United States, though, as the buildings grew taller, the options for evacuation became more complicated. High-profile, horrific building fires were a nearly constant plague in factories, tenements, office buildings, and theaters. The external fire escape seemed obvious to many: Bolt a metal staircase to the outside of the building with a landing below a window on each floor. Fire escapes became an element of American culture in many ways beyond simple safety equipment. They serve as dramatic devices in films and plays, provide a scenic place for urbanites to get some fresh air, and they impart a quintessential character on the skylines of our oldest cities. But it turns out that we’ve pretty much never agreed on how well they actually work (if at all) or whether they were ever the right solution to the problem. And while many older buildings still have the original ones installed and maintained, they’ve slowly started disappearing. The story of their decline is a fascinating case study in how building codes actually work. I’m Grady and this is Practical Engineering. An important thing to keep in mind about any safety devices in buildings, including elaborate metal contraptions that serve as fire escapes: owners don’t just install this stuff out of the goodness of their hearts. And I don’t mean that as a dig on the owners. It’s just very difficult to weigh the costs and benefits of safety

More posts by Scott Helme. SCOTT HELME 20 OCT 2026 • 7 MIN READ One of eMudhra's certificate authority private keys is the number 4. Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4... Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second. What happened On Saturday 17th October a security researcher reported to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and eMudhra that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. Chrome pushed a CRLSet update blocking them that evening and Mozilla blocked them in Firefox via OneCRL a few hours later. On Tuesday 20th, Mozilla announced it publicly and shipped an NSS update removing the eMudhra root, and Chrome confirmed the root is going in Chrome Root Store v43. The eight intermediates are six TLS issuing CAs (DV, OV and EV, two generations each) and two code-signing CAs, all created in April 2025. Every one of them was also cross-signed by Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root in May 2025. That's the "what", but it's the "how" that's the interesting part, and it was summed up in one line on the thread by Ian Carroll: They are inherently weak single-byte keys that anyone can factor, and the issue cannot be contained. What a private key actually is These are elliptic-curve keys on the P-384 curve. The private key is just a number, d. The public key, the thing that goes in the certificate for the world to see, is d × G, where G is a fixed point on the curve that everyone uses and "×" means adding G to itself

page.description: Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. In this post, we preview data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude.
page.text_excerpt: Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code Published Oct 20, 2026 Team Frontier Red Team Chris Rohlf Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose. Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability. Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. page.text_excerpt: NICOLAS MATTIA Setting up SSH keys on macOS with Touch ID October 19, 2026 In the first part of this post I’ll show a simple, secure way to create an SSH key on Mac (it’s 3 commands, including support for GitHub). In the second part I’ll dig deeper and explain what’s actually happening for the curious reader. Macs have a built-in so-called Secure Enclave, where we can create “identities” that simply cannot be stolen (unless maybe you’ve made enemies with a nation state). Those identities are protected with Touch ID and can be used for SSH authentication. There are some great benefits about using this over traditional SSH key files: The private material cannot be extracted, is never shown, cannot be stolen, You get prompted whenever the identity is used, No key files (like ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and friends) littering the file system; and there’s no risk of mistakenly deleting them either. This extra security will be in effect whenever you use SSH, including git-over-ssh like GitHub. It’s great that advanced security tech is available by default on some of the most widely distributed computers in the world! A few years ago stuff like this could only be found at CERN and/or in Dan Brown novels. Let’s see how it can be set up on your consumer-grade Mac. It is essential that the human interface be designed for ease of use, so that users routinely and automatically apply the protection mechanisms correctly. If you look up science on Wikipedia, here’s what hits you: Science is a systematic discipline that builds and organises knowledge in the form of testable hypotheses and predictions about the universe. - Wikipedia Now, go and grab a random arXiv paper. October, 19th 2026 8 min read Sometimes you need to know how long a video is without downloading the entire file. This is common in video processing services, upload validators, and applications that charge users based on video length. Downloading a 500 MB video just to read its duration isn’t particularly efficient. Fortunately, MP4 stores metadata in a structure that can often be retrieved with a small HTTP request. There’s one catch: not every MP4 stores its duration in the same way. How MP4 stores video duration An MP4 file is made up of structures called boxes. Each box has a type and size. Some of the important ones are: ftyp: identifies the file format. moov: contains movie metadata. mvhd: stores movie-level timing information. mdat: contains encoded media data. moof: describes a media fragment. mfra: may contain a random-access index for fragments. In a regular MP4 file, the mvhd box contains two values: timescale tells us how many time units represent one second, while duration tells us how many units the movie lasts. The calculation is simple: JS Copy const durationTicks = 540_000; const timescale = 30_000; const durationInSeconds = durationTicks / timescale; console.log(durationInSeconds); // 18 For example, a duration of 540,000 ticks with a timescale of 30,000 gives us 18 seconds. Sontag “knows everything, but she understands nothing,” the influential photographer, and photography teacher, Lisette Model reportedly said. Sontag’s Whitmanesque vision of American photographic history as finding beauty and value in increasingly unlikely places, a project she sees as culminating in Walker Evans’s surveys of the American scene, is tendentious but compelling. But the most influential essay in the book is motivated by a deep animus, even hatred — not just for the medium, but for Diane Arbus, then arguably the most famous and controversial photographer in America. Sontag reduces Arbus’s ambivalent images to Surrealist suffering porn for the bien pensant, and leaps to wild generalizations: photography is essentially about “aggression,” the photographer is a “supertourist” in subcultures and underworlds. But Sontag’s book, and with it the whole history of photography, might have been different if she’d turned her attention to the work of her close friend Peter Hujar. Hujar himself bitterly suggested that Sontag didn’t mention him in the book because he wasn’t famous enough, and indeed it’s only been in the last few years that he’s become anything more than a photographer’s photographer.
